rv.q: An exhilarating reading that reframes the psychological landscape of the original for our own image-obsessed age.
After this soul-baring, roof-raising performance it would be churlish to disagree.
As a piece of live theatre this is truly awesome stuff.
It’s the kind of uncompromisingly brilliant performance that makes you want to use cliches like “tour de force”.

There is a magnificence in simplicity, and Scherzinger’s Norma, initially drawing herself regally downstage, in black dress and shades, her dark hair long with a soupcon of the untamed warrior, has a poise that thrills.
This frisky, occasionally bonkers production easily exceeded my expectations for an evening watching a histrionic Lloyd Webber musical.
Genre swamps character: it is a dazzling argument, but more hologram than heart.
So why, with all these riches, does it leave this critic so removed and restless?
This is a Sunset Boulevard for a new generation.
Endlessly fierce and hip, this bold interpretation of the material dazzles with its transformation of the musical’s bare bones into a tragic feast of profound power.
This might not be the Sunset Boulevard you expect, but it is vibrant live theatre.
Scherzinger nails Norma's two showstoppers — one in each act — shedding sunglasses as she lifts the defiant "With One Look" to the rafters and beyond.
By the end, for all its technical dazzlement, you’re left thinking, have we been watching “Sunset Boulevard” or “Everybody’s Talking About Jamie Lloyd”?
Overall the show feels like a Gothic opera staged in an underground car park during a blackout.
No matter if you have seen this show before.
Sunset Boulevard never really gels as a whole.
The revival, directed by Jamie Lloyd, took a daringly austere approach, forgoing grand stage machinery in favor of a largely monochrome scheme.

Lloyd, who is known for his innovative work across recent adaptations of The Seagull, A Doll’s House and Cyrano de Bergerac, as well as the National Theatre’s The Effect, certainly provides blue sky thinking for how theatre can incorporate film technology in new ways. It’s exciting to think what he may have next.

Despite the source material suggesting the need for decaying glamour, director Lloyd and company have opted to dispense almost entirely with the need for sets or props. Instead the audience are presented with an almost entirely black stage, occasionally augmented by a semi-translucent curtain of shi...

Literally black-and-white (like the 1950. Billy Wilder film on which the musical is based) until its blood-splattered denouement, the production is a stunner. If little about the Evita rejig made sense, everything here is in service to the story.

cn.t: Jamie Lloyd's audacious, stripped-back reimagining divides critics, but Scherzinger's star turn wins widespread praise. The stark, film-noir aesthetic and innovative camera work dazzle some while feeling gimmicky to others.
